cards.apply: Keep a simple record of favours given and received with key contacts, and make sure your side of the ledger stays generous.
cards.meaning: Grooming partners and cleaner fish show that 'you scratch my back, I'll scratch mine' can evolve between non-relatives. The risk is cheats who take help and never return it, so cooperators must remember and punish them.
cards.text: Reciprocity lets unrelated animals cooperate

cards.apply: In a long-term relationship, open with cooperation, respond in kind to bad faith, and forgive quickly once behaviour improves.
cards.meaning: In a chapter added to the 1989 edition, Dawkins discusses Robert Axelrod's tournaments, where 'Tit for Tat' (cooperate first, then copy the other player) beat cleverer strategies. Being nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear won over repeated games.
cards.text: Nice guys can finish first

cards.apply: Pick one idea you want to spread at work and make it easy to copy: short, memorable, and easy to repeat.
cards.meaning: Dawkins coined 'meme' for units of culture, such as tunes, catchphrases or fashions, that spread by imitation from brain to brain. Memes compete and mutate like genes, and may spread whether or not they help the people carrying them.
cards.text: Ideas replicate too: the birth of the 'meme'

cards.apply: Look at what your daily habits build outside you (files, tools, routines) and change one that works against your long-term goals.
cards.meaning: In the closing chapter of later editions, Dawkins previews his 'extended phenotype': a gene's effects can extend outside its body, as with beaver dams or parasites altering their hosts. He also argues humans, uniquely, can rebel against their replicators through foresight.
cards.text: Genes reach beyond the body

cards.apply: List three things your team does only because a successful rival does them. Ask what you would do if that rival didn't exist.
cards.meaning: Thiel's opening line: the next Bill Gates won't build an operating system and the next Google won't build a search engine. Copying a past winner's model only takes the world from 1 to n; real value comes from doing something new.
cards.text: Every moment in business happens only once.

cards.apply: For a company you follow, label each growth driver as 'copying' or 'creating'. Weight the creating ones more in your view of its long-term value.
cards.meaning: Thiel splits progress in two: horizontal (copying what works, i.e. globalisation) and vertical (inventing something new, i.e. technology). He argues the world over-rewards the first and that durable growth needs the second.
cards.text: Going from 0 to 1 beats going from 1 to n

cards.apply: Write one sentence answering this question about your industry. Then list the evidence that would prove you wrong.
cards.meaning: Thiel's favourite interview question. It is hard because it needs a view that is both true and unpopular, and saying it costs something. Every great business, he argues, is built around such a contrarian truth.
cards.text: What important truth do very few people agree with you on?

cards.apply: Pick one 'rule' your team treats as settled wisdom. Spend 15 minutes arguing the opposite case honestly.
cards.meaning: After 2000, Silicon Valley learned to move in small steps, stay lean, improve on competitors and focus on product over sales. Thiel argues the opposite of each is often truer: bold plans beat tinkering, and distribution matters.
cards.text: The dot-com lessons may be the wrong lessons

cards.apply: When screening a stock, ask how much of its margin would survive a well-funded copycat. Favour firms with no close substitute.
cards.meaning: In perfect competition, profits are competed away. Creative monopolies, firms so much better that no one offers a close substitute, keep their profits and can invest in the long term. Thiel sees this as the condition of every lasting business.
cards.text: Competition is for losers; monopoly is the goal

cards.apply: Rewrite a company's market definition two ways, narrowly and broadly. See which one its management prefers and ask why.
cards.meaning: Dominant firms describe their market as huge to avoid scrutiny, so Google calls itself a tech company, not a search engine. Small firms shrink their market definition to look special. Both stories hide the true competitive picture.
cards.text: Monopolies pretend to compete; rivals pretend to be unique

cards.apply: Score one holding or target company 0 to 3 on each of the four traits. A total under 5 means its moat needs a harder look.
cards.meaning: Proprietary technology at least ten times better than the next best, network effects, economies of scale, and branding. Together they let a firm stay dominant for years, which matters because most of its value lies in distant future cash flows.
cards.text: Durable monopolies share four traits

cards.apply: Name the smallest group of customers your product could win outright this quarter. Focus one initiative on just them.
cards.meaning: A startup should first own a tiny market, as Amazon did with books and PayPal with eBay power sellers, then widen in concentric circles. Chasing a big market at the start means facing big rivals with nothing that sets you apart.
cards.text: Start small, dominate a niche, then expand

cards.apply: Write down one specific outcome you want in 12 months and the three steps that make it likely. Swap one vague goal for it.
cards.meaning: Thiel faults a culture that expects the future to improve but makes no concrete plans, relying on diversification and process instead. Great companies, he says, are built by people with a specific vision they work to make real.
cards.text: Be a definite optimist: plan, don't just hope

cards.apply: Rank your portfolio or project list by realistic upside, not probability. Put more attention on the top one or two.
cards.meaning: The best investment in a successful fund can return more than all the others combined. So each bet should be able to return the whole fund. The same logic applies to careers: a few decisions drive most of the results.
cards.text: Venture returns follow a power law

cards.apply: Check one partnership or deal you're in: are ownership, control and incentives clearly written down? Fix any gap this week.
cards.meaning: Thiel's law: a startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed. Choosing co-founders, splitting ownership, control and pay, and aligning everyone for the long term matter more than almost anything that follows.
cards.text: Foundations can't be fixed later

cards.apply: For a company you analyse, work out what it costs to win a customer and what that customer is worth. If the first is near the second, be cautious.
cards.meaning: Engineers often assume the best product wins on its own. Thiel argues poor sales and distribution, not weak products, cause most failures, and that a business needs at least one channel that works, from viral growth to direct sales.
cards.text: Great products still need great distribution

cards.apply: Before using a number in your next memo, write down who produced it, whether they saw it first-hand, and what they gain if it's wrong.
cards.meaning: Writing in the 2nd century AD, Arrian built his history mainly on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, who both marched with Alexander. He says he chose them because they were eyewitnesses and because a king like Ptolemy had more reason than most to keep to the truth.
cards.text: Trust the sources who had the most to lose by lying

cards.apply: Notice where one visible, consistent response to a broken commitment would prevent many future ones. Decide in advance what yours will be.
cards.meaning: When Thebes revolted in 335 BC, Alexander took the city and had it razed, sparing only temples and, by tradition, the poet Pindar's house. The brutal lesson kept the rest of Greece quiet while he left for Asia.
cards.text: Alexander made an example of Thebes to secure Greece

cards.apply: This week, take on the hardest, least glamorous piece of a team project yourself, and let the team see you do it.
cards.meaning: In his first battle against the Persians (334 BC), Alexander led the cavalry charge across the river himself and was nearly killed in the melee. Arrian shows a leader whose men followed because he took the same risks they did.
cards.text: At the Granicus, the commander rode into the river first

cards.apply: Pick a problem your team has 'tried everything' on. List the rules everyone assumes, then test what happens if one of them is ignored.
cards.meaning: Arrian gives two versions of the Gordian knot: the famous sword stroke, and Aristobulus's account that Alexander simply pulled out the pin holding the knot. Either way, he refused to play by the puzzle's assumed rules.
cards.text: He struck the cord with his sword and cut it through

cards.apply: When analysing a competitor or a deal, find the single point everything depends on: one founder, one customer, one contract. Weigh it accordingly.
cards.meaning: Arrian shows Alexander leading his right wing across the river at a run and driving for the Persian king. In a huge army held together by one man, breaking the centre of command broke the whole force.
cards.text: At Issus he aimed his charge straight at Darius

cards.apply: If a key goal keeps failing, ask what slow, unglamorous groundwork would make it inevitable, then schedule the first piece.
cards.meaning: The island city of Tyre seemed untakeable, so Alexander had a causeway built out to it and attacked from ships and siege towers. The siege took about seven months in 332 BC, but it left no Persian naval base behind him.
cards.text: Tyre fell because he built a road across the sea

cards.apply: Before your next big push, list what could hit you from behind: an unpaid vendor, a weak control, a key-person risk. Close one first.
cards.meaning: After Issus, Alexander didn't race inland after Darius. He first took the Mediterranean coast and Egypt, cutting off the Persian fleet, and only then marched east to win at Gaugamela in 331 BC.
cards.text: He secured the coast before chasing the Persian king

cards.apply: When you win a negotiation, give the other side something to keep their dignity. Today's opponent is often tomorrow's partner.
cards.meaning: After the hard-fought battle at the Hydaspes (326 BC), the defeated Indian king Porus gave this reply when asked how he wished to be treated. Arrian says Alexander was pleased, restored his kingdom and later enlarged it, gaining a loyal ally.
cards.text: Treat me, O Alexander, in a kingly way!

cards.apply: Recognise one long-serving colleague publicly this week for steady work that never gets headlines.
cards.meaning: Alexander founded two cities near the Hydaspes: Nicaea for the victory, and Bucephala for his horse, who Arrian says died of toil and old age, not wounds. It shows how Alexander tied loyalty and memory to his campaigns.
cards.text: Even Bucephalas got a city named after him

cards.apply: Ask the people doing the work whether a goal is still realistic, and listen. Ambition without buy-in stalls.
cards.meaning: Coenus closed his speech at the Hyphasis River with this line, when the exhausted army refused to march further into India. Alexander sulked for days, then turned back: the limit of his empire was set by his men, not his ambition.
cards.text: Self-control in the midst of success is the noblest of all virtues, O king!

cards.apply: Look at a plan you're championing: who bears the cost if it goes wrong? Make sure you share that cost, not just the credit.
cards.meaning: On the way back from India, Alexander led his army through the Gedrosian desert, and Arrian describes heavy losses to heat and thirst. Famously, offered a little water in a helmet, Alexander poured it out rather than drink while his men could not.
cards.text: The Gedrosian desert march cost a huge share of the army

cards.apply: Write a short review of a leader you admire: three things to copy, one thing to avoid. Keep both lists honest.
cards.meaning: Arrian condemns acts like the drunken killing of his friend Cleitus, yet credits Alexander for openly regretting his mistakes, which he saw as rare among kings. Admiration, he shows, need not mean blindness.
cards.text: Arrian praises Alexander but refuses to excuse his crimes
